scenes.head: Linking the statements
scenes.sub: The income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement are three views of one set of events, so a model must tie them together: profit to equity, schedules to the balance sheet, and every balance sheet change to cash. Link Lantern’s three statements, make them balance, find out why a model does not, and test Coastline’s covenant.

segs.say: Linking the statements. The income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement are three views of one set of events, so a model must tie them together: profit to equity, schedules to the balance sheet, and every balance sheet change to cash. Link Lantern’s three statements, make them balance, find out why a model does not, and test Coastline’s covenant.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Construct a forecast income statement below EBITDA: depreciation, interest, tax with losses carried forward, and net income.
Build the balance sheet from the schedules and roll equity forward with profit, dividends and new shares.
Prepare the cash flow statement by the indirect method from the income statement and the changes in the balance sheet, and link its closing cash to the balance sheet.
Diagnose a balance sheet that does not balance, using the size and sign of the difference.
Test a current-ratio covenant from the linked statements and explain the result to a lender.

scenes.head: Ana now has every piece: the forecast to EBITDA, working capital, fixed assets, and the loans.

segs.say: Ana now has every piece: the forecast to EBITDA, working capital, fixed assets, and the loans. Coastline’s credit officer will look at none of them on their own. She will open the balance sheet for 31 December 2028, check that it balances, read the cash, and divide current assets by current liabilities. This lesson puts the pieces together so that she can.

chapters.title: Three statements, one set of events

scenes.head: A three-statement model forecasts the income statement, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement together, linked so that each event appears…

segs.say: A three-statement model forecasts the income statement, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement together, linked so that each event appears consistently in all three. F02 showed the links in a set of accounts; a model reproduces them with formulas. There are only a few, and every model has the same ones.
Net income from the income statement increases retained earnings on the balance sheet, and starts the cash flow statement.
Depreciation is an expense in the income statement, reduces property and equipment on the balance sheet, and is added back in the cash flow statement because it uses no cash.
Working capital balances come from the working capital schedule; their changes appear in operating cash flow.
Capital spending adds to property and equipment and is an investing cash outflow.
Debt: drawings and repayments change the loans on the balance sheet and are financing cash flows; interest is an expense; the current portion is a current liability.
Equity: new shares add to common stock and to financing cash; dividends reduce retained earnings and cash.
Cash: the closing cash in the cash flow statement is the cash on the balance sheet.

scenes.head: If every link is right, the balance sheet balances by itself, without any plug.

segs.say: If every link is right, the balance sheet balances by itself, without any plug. That is why the balance check, total assets minus total liabilities and equity, is the most important row in a model: it must be zero in every period, and when it is not, a link is broken.

scenes.head: The income statement continues from lesson 3’s EBITDA.

segs.say: The income statement continues from lesson 3’s EBITDA. Depreciation comes from the fixed asset schedule and interest from the debt schedule, giving pre-tax profit. Tax is 25% of pre-tax profit, with one complication: 2028 is a loss. A company that makes a tax loss pays no tax that year, and the loss can be carried forward to reduce the taxable profit of later years. Lantern’s 2028 loss of $19,292 is set against 2029’s profit, so 2029’s tax is 25% of $18,005 instead of $37,297. The model keeps the unused loss in its own row, a tax loss carryforward, and ignores the limits some tax systems put on how much can be used in one year.
Lantern’s forecast income statement below EBITDA (dollars)

scenes.head: Every line of the forecast balance sheet comes from a schedule or a roll-forward, never from a typed number.

segs.say: Every line of the forecast balance sheet comes from a schedule or a roll-forward, never from a typed number. Cash comes from the cash flow statement. Working capital lines come from lesson 4’s schedule, property and equipment from its roll-forward, debt and the current portion from lesson 5. The cafés’ right-of-use asset and lease liability run down together. Common stock rises by Hollis Avery’s $75,000, and retained earnings roll forward: last year’s balance, plus net income, less dividends.
Lantern’s balance sheet at 31 December (dollars)

scenes.head: The cash flow statement is built by the indirect method from the other two statements.

segs.say: The cash flow statement is built by the indirect method from the other two statements. Operating cash flow starts from net income, adds back depreciation, and adjusts for each change in working capital and in interest owed. Investing cash flow is capital spending. Financing cash flow is new loans and shares, less repayments and dividends, plus or minus the line of credit. For 2028: operating cash flow is −19,292 + 35,979 + 8,589 + 6,630 − 453 = 31,453 dollars; investing, $-105,000; financing, $82,016.
Lantern’s forecast cash flow statement (dollars)

scenes.head: Inside each forecast year the model calculates in a fixed order, and seeing it makes the links easier to follow and to check.

segs.say: Inside each forecast year the model calculates in a fixed order, and seeing it makes the links easier to follow and to check. First the operations: revenue, costs and EBITDA (lesson 3), then the working capital balances and the fixed asset schedule (lesson 4). Then the loans whose terms are fixed: their interest and repayments for the year (lesson 5). With depreciation and interest known, the income statement can be finished down to net income, with tax after any loss carried forward. Next comes cash before the line of credit: last year’s cash, plus operating cash flow, less capital spending, plus new loans and shares, less repayments and dividends. Only then does the revolver decide how much to draw or repay, and only then is cash final. Last of all, the balance sheet is assembled and checked.

scenes.head: The order matters because each step uses only results from the steps before it, or from the year before.

segs.say: The order matters because each step uses only results from the steps before it, or from the year before. That is what keeps the model free of loops. The line of credit’s interest is the one place a loop could form, and charging it on the opening balance puts it in the first group of calculations instead of the last.

scenes.head: Once the statements link, the forecast can be read as one story.

segs.say: Once the statements link, the forecast can be read as one story. In 2028 Lantern loses money, builds the second kitchen and launches Cold Brew, and finances it with the term loan and Hollis’s equity, ending the year with cash at the $15,000 minimum. From 2029 profit returns, the line of credit is repaid, and cash builds: $33,490 at the end of 2029 and $162,280 by 2032, after dividends of 30% of each year’s profit from 2030. Debt falls from $72,266 at the end of 2028 to $3,562 by 2032. Property and equipment fall as the 2028 investment is depreciated, until the café refit in 2032.

scenes.head: Two features deserve a comment in the model’s notes.

segs.say: Two features deserve a comment in the model’s notes. The large cash balance from 2030 is a question for Ana and Hollis: hold it for a third kitchen or another café, pay more out, or repay the term loan early? A model does not decide that, but it makes the question visible. And total assets jump in 2032 because the cafés’ leases are renewed: the right-of-use asset and the lease liability both return to their original size, which changes the balance sheet but not cash or profit.

chapters.title: When the balance sheet does not balance

scenes.head: Every modeller builds a model that does not balance at some point.

segs.say: Every modeller builds a model that does not balance at some point. The difference itself is the best clue to the cause, and a few checks find most errors.
Check the first forecast year first. If the opening balance sheet balances and the first year does not, the error is in that year’s links; later years inherit it.

If the difference equals a single amount in the model, that amount is probably missing from one side: a balance sheet change with no cash flow (a new loan added to debt but not to financing cash), or a cash flow with no balance sheet change.
If the difference is twice an amount, that amount probably has the wrong sign somewhere: an increase in receivables added in the cash flow statement instead of subtracted.
If the difference grows each year by the same amount, a recurring flow is missing, such as depreciation not added back, or dividends not deducted from retained earnings.
Never plug the difference. A typed adjustment that makes the check zero hides the error and breaks the model the next time an input changes.

scenes.head: With the balance sheet built, the covenant is one row: current assets divided by current liabilities, using Coastline’s definition, which leaves…

segs.say: With the balance sheet built, the covenant is one row: current assets divided by current liabilities, using Coastline’s definition, which leaves lease liabilities out. At 31 December 2028 Lantern’s current assets are $58,984 and its current liabilities $58,382: a current ratio of 1.01. The covenant requires at least 1.2. From 2029 the ratio is 1.63 and rising.

scenes.head: The model has found a problem

segs.say: The model has found a problem. Lantern’s base case breaches its covenant at the end of 2028. The causes are visible in the model: a loss year, cash held only at the $15,000 minimum, the line of credit still drawn, and $20,027 of term loan, van note and brewer principal falling due within a year. F05 checked the ratio only at 31 March 2028; the full model shows a later quarter that fails. And Coastline tests the covenant every quarter end, so an annual model can only show year ends: the quarters inside 2028 need checking too. This is what models are for: finding a problem in February, on paper, instead of in December, with the bank.

scenes.head: Retained earnings roll-forward

segs.say: Retained earnings roll-forward: REₜ = REₜ₋₁ + Net incomeₜ − Dividendsₜ.
REₜ: Retained earnings at the end of year t ($).
It assumes this: No other changes to retained earnings (no restatements).

scenes.head: Operating cash flow, indirect method

segs.say: Operating cash flow, indirect method: CFO = NI + Depreciation − ΔOperating assets + ΔOperating liabilities.
ΔOperating assets: Increase in receivables, inventory and other operating current assets ($).
ΔOperating liabilities: Increase in payables, accrued wages, interest owed, unearned revenue and taxes owed ($).
It assumes this: No other non-cash items (no gains on disposals, no deferred tax).

scenes.head: Closing cash

segs.say: Closing cash: Cashₜ = Cashₜ₋₁ + CFOₜ + CFIₜ + CFFₜ.
CFIₜ: Investing cash flow (capital spending, negative) ($).
CFFₜ: Financing cash flow (loans and shares in, repayments and dividends out) ($).
It assumes this: This figure, not a separate calculation, is the cash on the balance sheet.

scenes.head: The balance check

segs.say: The balance check: Checkₜ = Total assetsₜ − (Total liabilitiesₜ + Equityₜ) = 0.
Checkₜ: Must be zero in every period; anything else is a broken link ($).
It assumes this: No plugs: the check is a test, not a balancing figure.

scenes.head: Taxable profit with a loss carried forward

segs.say: Taxable profit with a loss carried forward: Taxableₜ = max (0, EBTₜ − Loss carried forwardₜ₋₁).
EBTₜ: Pre-tax profit in year t ($).
Loss carried forwardₜ₋₁: Earlier losses not yet used ($).
It assumes this: Losses can be used in full in any later year (some tax systems cap the yearly use).

scenes.head: Rolling retained earnings forward

segs.say: Lantern’s retained earnings were $42,818 at the end of 2027. The model forecasts net income of $(19,292) in 2028 and $32,795 in 2029, with no dividends in either year (2028 is a loss, and 2029’s dividend is 30% of 2028’s profit, which is nil). Find retained earnings at the end of 2028 and 2029, and total equity, given common stock of $95,000 after Hollis’s investment.

scenes.head: Rolling retained earnings forward

segs.say: Step 3. Equity at the end of 2028: common stock 95,000 + retained earnings 23,526 = 118,526.
Step 4. 2030’s dividend will be 30% of 2029’s profit: 0.30 × 32,795 = 9,839, deducted from retained earnings in 2030.

scenes.head: Rolling retained earnings forward

segs.say: Retained earnings $23,526 (2028) and $56,321 (2029); equity $118,526 at the end of 2028.
The loss reduces retained earnings, but Hollis’s $75,000 more than offsets it: equity nearly doubles in 2028, which is part of what makes the debt look safe to a lender.

chapters.title: Example: Lantern’s 2028 cash flow, from the pieces

scenes.head: Lantern’s 2028 cash flow, from the pieces

segs.say: For 2028 the model shows a net loss of $19,292, depreciation of $35,979, working capital assets falling by $8,589 (the contract asset is collected), working capital liabilities rising by $6,630, interest owed falling by $453, capital spending of $105,000, the $60,000 term loan, Hollis’s $75,000, loan repayments of $34,725 and the line of credit repaid by $18,259. Lantern started the year with $6,531 of cash. Build the cash flow and find closing cash.

scenes.head: Lantern’s 2028 cash flow, from the pieces

segs.say: Step 2. Investing: −105,000.
Step 4. Change in cash: 31,453 − 105,000 + 82,016 = 8,469; closing cash 6,531 + 8,469 = 15,000, the minimum the revolver aims for.

scenes.head: Lantern’s 2028 cash flow, from the pieces

segs.say: Operating $31,453, investing −$105,000, financing $82,016; cash rises $8,469 to $15,000.

Despite the loss, operations produce cash, helped by depreciation and the contract asset’s collection. The kitchen is paid for by the term loan and Hollis’s money, which also repay the old note, the brewer plan and most of the line of credit.

chapters.title: Example: Telling Coastline about the covenant

scenes.head: Telling Coastline about the covenant

segs.say: At 31 December 2028 the model shows current assets of $58,984 and current liabilities (excluding leases) of $58,382. The covenant requires a current ratio of at least 1.2. Test it, and work out how much more cash Lantern would need at the year end, financed from a long-term source, to pass.

scenes.head: Telling Coastline about the covenant

segs.say: Step 1. Current ratio: 58,984 ÷ 58,382 = 1.010, below 1.2: a breach.
Step 2. To pass, current assets must reach 1.2 × 58,382 = 70,058.
Step 3. Extra cash needed: 70,058 − 58,984 = 11,075, if it adds nothing to current liabilities (a longer or larger term loan, say, with little principal due in 2029; more equity; or less spending).
Step 4. Cash from the line of credit would not help: each dollar drawn adds a dollar to both current assets and current liabilities, which leaves the ratio near 1.

scenes.head: Telling Coastline about the covenant

segs.say: A current ratio of 1.01: a breach. Roughly $11,075 more cash from a long-term source would bring it to 1.2.
Ana should raise this with Coastline now, with the model, and a fix: a larger term loan, a covenant holiday for 2028, or a later Cold Brew launch. Module 3 tests those options as scenarios.

scenes.head: Coastline’s covenant at 31 December 2028 (first-order effects)

segs.say: The covenant at 31 December 2028, as a Formula Explorer. Raise the minimum cash, add a larger term loan, or delay some of 2028’s capital spending, and see which actually moves the current ratio past 1.2. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Plugging the difference

segs.say: Plugging the difference. A typed number that makes the balance check zero hides a broken link. Find the cause; the model will be wrong again the moment an input changes.

scenes.head: Calculating cash twice

segs.say: Calculating cash twice. If the balance sheet’s cash is worked out separately from the cash flow statement, the two can disagree. Link the balance sheet’s cash to the cash flow statement’s closing cash.

scenes.head: Forgetting a flow that changes a balance

segs.say: Forgetting a flow that changes a balance. Every change in a balance sheet line needs a cash flow or a profit item. A loan added to debt without a financing inflow, or dividends paid in cash but not deducted from retained earnings, breaks the balance.

scenes.head: Taxing a loss

segs.say: Taxing a loss. A loss year pays no tax, and its loss reduces later years’ taxable profit. A model that books a negative tax or ignores the carryforward misstates cash.

scenes.head: Reading the covenant with the wrong definition

segs.say: Reading the covenant with the wrong definition. Covenants use the loan agreement’s definitions. Coastline’s current ratio leaves lease liabilities out; using the accounting current ratio would give a different answer.

scenes.head: Assuming the line of credit fixes a current ratio

segs.say: Assuming the line of credit fixes a current ratio. Borrowing short-term to hold cash adds equally to current assets and current liabilities. Only long-term money or less spending improves the ratio.

scenes.head: In practice the balance check is the first thing anyone receiving a model looks at, and a model that does not balance is sent back unread.

segs.say: In practice the balance check is the first thing anyone receiving a model looks at, and a model that does not balance is sent back unread. Bankers, investors and auditors also check that the cash flow statement’s closing cash equals the balance sheet’s, and that retained earnings roll forward from net income and dividends, because those three tests catch most broken links.

scenes.head: Covenant tests are standard outputs in any model that supports a loan.

segs.say: Covenant tests are standard outputs in any model that supports a loan. Lenders set covenants with covenant headroom over the borrower’s forecast; a forecast that shows a breach, or very little headroom, changes the conversation before the loan is signed. Borrowers who show their lender a problem early, with a solution, usually get a better hearing than those whose lender finds it in the quarterly accounts.

scenes.head: Ana’s model now balances in every year and produces all three statements.

segs.say: Ana’s model now balances in every year and produces all three statements. It also shows her something she did not expect: at the end of 2028 Lantern’s current ratio is 1.01, below Coastline’s 1.2. Module 3 values the business from the same forecast and uses scenarios to find a financing plan that passes the covenant in every year.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A three-statement model links net income to retained earnings, schedules to the balance sheet, and every balance sheet change to cash.
Below EBITDA: depreciation from the fixed asset schedule, interest from the debt schedule, and tax on profit after losses carried forward.
Every balance sheet line comes from a schedule or a roll-forward; retained earnings = last year + net income − dividends.
Build the cash flow statement by the indirect method, and link its closing cash to the balance sheet.
The balance check must be zero every period; diagnose a difference from its size and sign, and never plug it.
Test covenants with the loan agreement’s definitions; short-term borrowing does not repair a current ratio.
Lantern’s base case breaches the 1.2 covenant at the end of 2028 (1.01), a problem the linked model finds before it happens.
